extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for creating consistent, authentic character voice in fiction, including exercises and tools (backstories, dialogue review, interviews, and observation) to ensure each character sounds distinct and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Voice is the character’s way of seeing the world — not just word selection but how the character interprets and responds to events internally. In a book you have the author’s voice, the character’s speaking voice, and the character’s internal voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal dialogue influences how they speak and what they choose to say; treat voice as a filter created by past experiences. Keep the distinction between author voice, speaking voice, and internal voice clear so each functions appropriately in the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of Voice (creates reader trust)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency creates trust: voice consistency creates trust with the reader. The reader will detect the smallest deviation in voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goal: create voices so distinct that each character can be identified without a tag line. Watch for deviations that break reader trust; ensure internal and spoken voices align with established backstory and personality. Use targeted revision (see Dialogue Folder exercise) to correct inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a Backstory for Each Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Know thy character’s past—every character is defined by past experiences and motivations usually lie in past events. As a writer you must know the backstory even if you don’t share it with readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A backstory prevents one-dimensional caricatures and helps you hear the character’s voice. Exercise: Create a character “bible” (a note or folder per main character). Suggested contents for the bible: Name and basic demographics; History (including parents, siblings); Ambitions for the future; Moral code; Dialogue (collected examples). Use a note-taking app (e.g., Evernote) to store files, clips, audio, and images. Quoted guidance: “Even if you find the bad guy generally repulsive, you need to be able to put yourself so thoroughly into his shoes while you’re writing him that, just for those moments, you almost believe his slant yourself.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Do a Character Study / Embody the Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Research the character so thoroughly that their responses feel instinctive — they’ve lived an entire life in a three-dimensional alternate universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time observing how the character would act and respond to stimuli. Exercise: Be the character for a day — ‘put on your character as you would a suit’ and spend the day responding to the world as that character to internalize choices and reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hone Internal Dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: A character’s voice is largely defined by what they say to themselves; thoughts create voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether internal dialogue is self-deprecating, self-aggrandizing, sensitive, sarcastic, etc. Recognize that past events shape this internal filter (e.g., trauma may make a character fearful or reckless). Exercise: Mind read — while living as the character, document what they would think in different situations (breakfast, in traffic, at work, at dinner), and note how they would think it (tone, phrasing). Use these notes to inform both internal narration and spoken dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research How People Speak Naturally
rubrics_metrics.description: Your character probably won’t speak like you; research real speech to avoid unnatural, exaggerated dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read primary sources appropriate to the character (e.g., Victorian letters for historical characters) and observe cadence, word choice, slang, idioms, and rhythm. Avoid caricatured speech ('Ello Gov’na', 'aw shucks') unless deliberately justified. Exercise: Study speech patterns by observing people in public (malls, coffee shops, restaurants), paying attention to loudness, diction, slang, idioms, and sentence rhythm. Note that every character has a natural sentence-structure rhythm (short halting commands vs. trailing mumble); comedians’ impersonations are useful models for cadence and word choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on Authentic Dialogue (preserve voice in interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue between characters can weaken a character’s voice when one voice dominates; ensure each character retains distinct speech when interacting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within the character bible include a dedicated dialogue section. Exercise: Create a Dialogue Folder — after drafting, copy each character’s dialogue into a file, read for inconsistencies, repetition (favorite phrases, sentence structures, passive/active voice), and tweak lines to maintain consistency of voice. This lets you spot when a character sounds inauthentic or when one character over-idealizes another’s speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview the Character (comprehensive question set)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask detailed questions to surface facts, attitudes, and patterns that shape voice (political ideology, moral code, mannerisms, background).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided question list as a starting point; add more as needed. The page’s suggested questions to ask each main character include: How does he say hello? What is your character’s style of speech? What is the sound of your character’s voice? What is your character’s disposition? What are his morals and beliefs? Is he or she educated? How far? How old are they? How would the character be described physically by a stranger (include height, weight, ethnicity)? Where are they from? Has he lived there all of his life or has he moved? Who are their parents and what is their relationship with them like? Does your character look more like mom or dad? Does your character have siblings? Are they close to their siblings? Why or why not? What was the character’s childhood like? What is your character’s greatest success? What is your character’s greatest failure? How is your character’s outlook on life? In general, is he pessimistic? Optimistic? What are the three most important motivations for the character? What are the three most important fears for the character? What is your character’s profession? Is he or she a student? Are they happy or not with their profession? Why? What is your character’s hobby? What does he or she do for fun? Who are/ were his best friends? Does your character have a lot of friends? Does your character have any enemies? Is your character married? Dating? Why? What do they want from a relationship? Does he have any children? Who is the most significant person in your character’s life? What makes your character happy? What makes your character sad? What is the most important, defining event in your character’s life? Is your character predominantly passive or aggressive? Is he or she introverted or extroverted? Use answers to these questions to populate the character bible and to ground internal and spoken voice choices.
